sections.markdown:
## C — Yielding right-of-way, traffic control devices, steady and flashing signal meanings, warning signs, railroad crossing signs and rules, and work zone signs and controls
Knowledge domain: who yields to whom in South Carolina, what each steady and flashing signal light requires, how warning, railroad and work zone signs look and what they ask of a driver, and how to cross railroad tracks and pass through work zones safely.

FACT_ID: sec07-F01 | anchor: A01
Right-of-way rules tell drivers who should yield and in what order to enter and drive through an intersection or a similar situation when other drivers or pedestrians are present. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec07-F02 | anchor: A01
Nobody should assume the right-of-way is automatically theirs, because the situation and circumstances at each intersection always have to be considered. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec07-F03 | anchor: A01
Yield to pedestrians, bicyclists and other drivers who are still in the intersection. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec07-F04 | anchor: A01
Yield to a driver who is already at the intersection or arrives there before you, which the manual illustrates as the First Car Rule. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec07-F05 | anchor: A02
When you are making a left turn, yield to drivers in the opposing traffic lane. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec07-F06 | anchor: A02
At a four-way intersection controlled by stop signs, if you and another driver arrive at the same time, yield to the driver on your right, which the manual calls the Same Time Rule. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec07-F07 | anchor: A02
When you enter a public highway from a driveway or a private road, yield to the drivers already on that highway. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec07-F08 | anchor: A02
On an entrance or acceleration ramp, yield to drivers who are already on the limited access or interstate highway. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec07-F09 | anchor: A02
Traffic control devices include traffic signals, signs and pavement markings, plus directions given by law enforcement, highway personnel and school crossing guards. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec07-F10 | anchor: A02
Traffic signals are lights that tell you when or where to stop and go; they are usually at intersections, with red at the top, yellow in the middle and green at the bottom of a single device. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec07-F11 | anchor: A03
Some metropolitan areas use horizontal signals, with the red light on the left, yellow in the middle and green on the right. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec07-F12 | anchor: A03
A green light means you may go through the intersection with caution if it is clear to do so. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec07-F13 | anchor: A03
A steady yellow light follows the green and warns that the signal is about to turn red, so you should stop and wait for the next green. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec07-F14 | anchor: A03
If you are already inside the intersection when the light turns yellow, clear it as quickly as you can. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec07-F15 | anchor: A03
A red light means stop before entering the intersection and wait behind the stop line, crosswalk or intersection until the light turns green. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec07-F16 | anchor: A03
Traffic facing a red signal may turn right, except where a sign prohibits a right turn on red. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec07-F17 | anchor: A03
To turn right on red, stop before the crosswalk on the near side of the turn and yield to pedestrians lawfully in or next to it and to other traffic lawfully using the intersection. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec07-F18 | anchor: A03
A flashing yellow light means slow down and go ahead with caution, ready to stop for any traffic that may be entering the intersection. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec07-F19 | anchor: A04
At a flashing red light you come to a complete stop behind the stop line, crosswalk or intersection as at a stop sign, then look both ways and yield if required before entering. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec07-F20 | anchor: A04
Traffic signs give information on traffic rules, hazards, location, directions and roadway services, and their shape, color, symbols and words hint at the kind of message they carry. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec07-F21 | anchor: A04
Warning signs tell you about possible danger ahead, such as a need to slow down and be ready to stop, or a hazard or special situation on the road. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec07-F22 | anchor: A04
Most warning signs are diamond shaped and colored yellow, with their lettering or symbols in black. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec07-F23 | anchor: A04
Some warning signs, including those for school zones, school crossings and pedestrian crossings, may be fluorescent yellow. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec07-F24 | anchor: A04
Common warning signs pictured include Right Curve, Curvy Road Ahead, Cross Road Ahead, T-Intersection Ahead, Side Road Ahead and Y-Intersection Ahead. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec07-F25 | anchor: A05
Further warning signs pictured are Divided Highway Begins, Divided Highway Ends, Lane Ends, Merging Traffic, Added Lane and Traffic Signal Ahead. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec07-F26 | anchor: A05
The same page also pictures Slippery When Wet, Bicycle Crossing, Stop Sign Ahead, Pedestrian Crossing, Sharp Curve Ahead, School Crossing, Share the Road with Bicycles and Advisory Speed Around Curve signs. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec07-F27 | anchor: A06
A round yellow sign with an X symbol and black RR letters stands along the road before a highway-railroad grade crossing, telling you to slow down, look and listen for a train, and be ready to stop. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec07-F28 | anchor: A06
A white X-shaped sign printed with Railroad Crossing stands at the crossing itself, and when a train is approaching you must stop behind the stop line or before the crossing until it is clear. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec07-F29 | anchor: A06
At crossings with more than one track, the number of tracks is posted to warn that more than one train or railroad vehicle may be crossing. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec07-F30 | anchor: A07
Not every railroad grade crossing has lights. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec07-F31 | anchor: A07
When crossing railroad tracks, look both ways and cross quickly without stopping. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec07-F32 | anchor: A07
If a train is crossing the highway, wait until it is well down the track or until railroad lights and gates show it is safe to cross. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec07-F33 | anchor: A07
If traffic or a signal makes you stop as you approach railroad tracks, halt at the stop line in front of the tracks. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec07-F34 | anchor: A07
If your vehicle ever gets stuck on a track, call the emergency phone number on the blue sign and give the crossing information. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec07-F35 | anchor: A07
Work zone signs are generally diamond or rectangular in shape and orange with black letters or symbols. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec07-F36 | anchor: A07
These signs alert you to construction, maintenance or emergency work and warn of workers, reduced speed zones, detours, slow construction equipment and poor or suddenly changing road surfaces. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec07-F37 | anchor: A08
Work zone signs pictured include Flagger Ahead, Workers Ahead, Road Construction Ahead, One Lane Road Ahead and Detour. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec07-F38 | anchor: A08
In a work zone a person with a sign or flag may tell you which way to go or to slow down or stop, and you must follow those instructions. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec07-F39 | anchor: A08
Barriers such as drums, cones and tubes, also called panels, keep traffic out of hazardous work areas and, along with signs and markings, guide you through the work zone. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec07-F40 | anchor: A08
Temporary traffic signals may be used in work zones, sometimes announced by a warning sign showing a signal symbol, and you stop at the white line if there is one. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0066]

Misconceptions: no driver is ever automatically owed the right-of-way; a steady yellow asks you to stop, not to speed up, unless you are already in the intersection; a flashing red works like a stop sign, while a steady red means waiting for green; right on red still needs a full stop first; not every railroad crossing has lights or a track-count sign.
Mnemonics: first to arrive goes first, and on a tie the car on the right goes; red over yellow over green from top to bottom, or red, yellow, green from left to right; yellow diamond warns, orange works.
Glossary: right-of-way means the privilege of going first that a driver must sometimes yield; traffic control device means any signal, sign, marking or official direction controlling traffic; grade crossing means a place where a highway crosses railroad tracks at the same level; flagger means a person in a work zone who directs traffic with a sign or flag; fluorescent yellow means the brighter yellow used on some school and pedestrian warning signs.

corpus_stability.reason: The South Carolina Driver's Manual prints a single edition line (Revised 06/2024) on its front cover; its disclaimer says legislative and SCDMV policy changes may make some content out of date until the agency incorporates them, and a possibly newer unlinked upload exists on the issuer site (freshness debt in the run jams), so the corpus is treated as revised at most about once a year, bound to the registered snapshot.
